key_insight: Echo-Memory isolates memory as the core failure mode in action-conditioned world models, showing that many apparent improvements come from confounded comparisons rather than truly better memory. It provides a controlled setup to fairly study how models remember and restore scene content after camera movement.
problem_solved: The paper addresses the difficulty of evaluating memory in world models, where objects or scenes can change silently after the camera leaves and returns. Existing memory methods are hard to compare because their benefits are mixed with differences in backbone design, training, retrieval, and evaluation.
method: Introduces a controlled benchmark/study for memory in action-conditioned world models that generate multi-segment videos from an initial frame, text prompt, and camera-action sequence.
Separates memory-specific effects from other factors so retrieval, architecture, and training choices can be compared more fairly.
Focuses on the failure case of returning to previously seen content, where a good model should preserve object identity and scene consistency over time.
impact: For practitioners, this helps identify whether a model truly has better memory or is only benefiting from setup differences. It also provides a clearer path for designing and evaluating world models that stay consistent over long, interactive sequences.
visual_elements: A timeline diagram showing a camera moving away from a scene and then returning, with the expected vs. changed object state.
A side-by-side comparison of model outputs highlighting memory failure versus preserved consistency.
A pipeline diagram of the world model inputs: first frame, text prompt, and action sequence leading to multi-segment video generation.
A comparison table or bar chart separating memory performance from backbone/training/retrieval confounders.
paper_title: Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models
paper_authors: Wayne King, Zeyue Xue, Yuxuan Bian, Jie Huang, Haoran Li
